passages.t: Paul, servant and apostle: the gospel about God's Son
passages.happening:
Paul opens the letter the way letters of his day opened: first the sender, then the people he writes to, then a greeting. But he stretches each part.

He names himself “a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle” (verse 1). An apostle is someone sent with a message. Paul has been “set apart for the gospel of God” (verse 1).

Then he says what that gospel is. God “promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures” (verse 2). It is about his Son, “who was a descendant of David according to the flesh” (verse 3), and who “was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (verse 4).

Through this Son, Paul says, he received grace and his calling as an apostle, to bring people from all the nations “to the obedience that comes from faith” (verse 5). The believers in Rome are among them, “called to belong to Jesus Christ” (verse 6).

Only then does he name them: “To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints” (verse 7). And he greets them: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
A letter in the Roman world began with a short formula: the sender's name, the receiver's name, and a one-word greeting, ‘greetings’. Paul turns the usual Greek greeting into grace, charis, God's free gift, and adds peace, the greeting of Jewish homes and the old Hebrew word shalom. Jew and Gentile are both in the first line.

The word ‘servant’ is the Greek doulos, which means slave. Rome was full of slaves. Paul chooses the lowest title in the city to describe himself. But Jewish hearers also knew it as an honoured title: Moses and David were each called the servant of the LORD.

‘Gospel’ means good news. In the Roman world the word was used for news about the emperor. An inscription set up at Priene, in what is now Turkey, about 9 BC, called the birthday of the emperor Augustus the beginning of good news for the world. Paul announces good news about a different Son, a king from David's line.

Verses 3 and 4 move in two balanced lines: descended from David ‘according to the flesh’, declared Son of God ‘by His resurrection’. Some scholars think Paul is quoting a short statement of faith the churches already knew. The resurrection did not make Jesus God's Son; it showed him to be the Son, with power.

‘Saints’ means holy ones, people set apart for God. It is not a name for unusually good Christians. Paul uses it for every believer in Rome.

‘The obedience that comes from faith’ can be read two ways: the obedience that grows out of trusting God, or the obedience that consists in trusting him. Both make sense. Paul uses the same phrase in the last lines of the letter (16:26), so the whole letter sits between them.
passages.ot:
Paul says the gospel was promised beforehand. He has a promise to David in mind. God told David through the prophet Nathan, “I will raise up your descendant after you” and “I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12), and then, “I will be his Father, and he will be My son” (2 Samuel 7:14). Psalm 2 says of the king God sets on Zion, “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (Psalm 2:7). In Acts, Paul applies that psalm to the day God raised Jesus (Acts 13:33).

The calling to the nations also has roots. God promised Abraham that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). And ‘servant of the LORD’ was the title of Moses (Joshua 1:1).

Paul's sense of being set apart echoes the call of Jeremiah: “before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jeremiah 1:5). Paul uses the same picture of himself in Galatians 1:15.
passages.hard: Was Jesus made God's Son when he rose? Verse 4 says he “was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead”. A few readers have taken it to mean he only became the Son then. But Paul has already called him “His Son” in verse 3, before he speaks of David or the resurrection. The church has read verse 4 as the moment the Son was shown openly, ‘with power’, for who he already was. The creeds confess him as the eternal Son, who became a descendant of David when he was born.
passages.asks: Paul tells you first whose he is, then what he does. Ask what title you would give yourself, and whether ‘servant of Christ Jesus’ could be part of it. And notice what he calls ordinary believers in a city he has never visited: loved by God, called, holy. Ask whether you believe that about yourself, and about the Christians you find hardest to love.

passages.happening:
Paul begins, as he usually does, with thanks: “First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed all over the world” (verse 8).

He calls God as his witness that he prays for them constantly, and that he keeps asking to come to them at last (verses 9-10). “For I long to see you so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you” (verse 11). Then he puts it more humbly: “that is, that you and I may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith” (verse 12).

He wants them to know that he has often planned to come and been prevented (verse 13). He hoped to see a harvest among them, as among the other Gentiles.

“I am obligated both to Greeks and non-Greeks, both to the wise and the foolish” (verse 14). That is why, he says, he is so eager to preach the gospel in Rome too (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Rome was the centre of the empire, and news from it travelled on every road and ship. A church in the capital would be talked about everywhere. ‘All over the world’ means the world Paul's hearers knew.

Notice Paul's tact. He did not found this church, and he had never met most of it. A famous apostle could have arrived as a master. Instead he corrects himself mid-sentence. He has something to give them, and they have something to give him. Faith strengthens faith in both directions.

Why was he prevented? He tells them later: he had been busy preaching where Christ was not known (15:20-22). This letter is partly his apology for being so long in coming.

‘Greeks and non-Greeks’ translates a common pair in the Greek world. Greek speakers called people who did not speak Greek barbaroi, outsiders whose speech they could not understand. ‘The wise and the foolish’ means the educated and the uneducated. Between them the two pairs take in everyone.

‘Obligated’ is the language of debt. Paul does not say he has a right to preach. He says he owes it. He has been given something that belongs to everyone, and he is paying it out.
passages.ot:
Paul's call to the nations carries the Servant's task in Isaiah: “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Paul and Barnabas quoted that verse when they turned to the Gentiles in Acts 13:47.

His eagerness to preach echoes another line of Isaiah he will quote later in this letter (10:15): “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news” (Isaiah 52:7).

The picture of a harvest also has old roots. In the Psalms, those who sow in tears reap with joy (Psalm 126:5-6).
passages.asks: Paul wanted to give something, and he also wanted to receive. Ask whether you come to other believers only to give, or only to get, and what it would be to be ‘mutually encouraged’. And ask who you owe the good news to. Paul said he owed it to the clever and the simple alike. Who are the people you would rather not be in debt to?

passages.t: ‘I am not ashamed of the gospel’
passages.happening:
Now Paul states the theme of the whole letter.

“I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (verse 16).

Then he gives the reason: “the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish” (verse 17). And he backs it with a line from the prophet Habakkuk: “The righteous will live by faith” (verse 17).

These two verses are the door into Romans. Almost everything that follows explains them: why the world needs saving, how God's righteousness is revealed, what faith is, and why the gospel is for the Jew first and also for the Greek.
passages.hearers:
Why would anyone be ashamed of the gospel? Because its centre was a man crucified. In the Roman world crucifixion was the punishment for slaves, bandits and rebels, a death meant to shame. To preach a crucified Jew as Lord in the capital of the empire was to invite laughter. Paul knows it, and says plainly that he is not ashamed.

‘Salvation’ means rescue. ‘The power of God’ means that the message does not only describe a rescue. When it is preached, God is at work in it.

‘First to the Jew, then to the Greek’. Here ‘Greek’ stands for everyone who is not Jewish. The order is about history, not favour. God made his promises to Israel first, and the Messiah came from Israel. So in Acts Paul goes first to the synagogue in each town. But the gospel is for ‘everyone who believes’.

‘The righteousness of God’ is the letter's key phrase. It may mean the right standing God gives to those who believe, or God's own faithfulness in keeping his promises and setting things right, or both. The book page sets out the readings.

‘From start to finish’ is the BSB's way of putting a short Greek phrase that says, word for word, ‘from faith to faith’. Readers take it in several ways: faith from beginning to end; from God's faithfulness to our faith; or from one believer to the next. On every reading, faith is how this righteousness is received.
passages.ot:
The quotation comes from Habakkuk 2:4. Habakkuk was a prophet in Judah who complained that God was not acting against evil. God's answer was worse than his question: he was raising up the Babylonians, “that ruthless and impetuous nation” (Habakkuk 1:6). Then God told Habakkuk to write down a vision and wait: “Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:3). And then: “the righteous will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4).

The Hebrew word behind ‘faith’ there means steadiness or faithfulness. In Habakkuk it describes the person who keeps trusting God while the promise is delayed and the world is falling apart. Paul takes the line and makes it the banner of the letter: the one who trusts God is the one God counts righteous, and that person will truly live.

The Psalms already joined God's righteousness and his salvation: “The LORD has proclaimed His salvation and revealed His righteousness to the nations” (Psalm 98:2).

Later Paul quotes Isaiah 28:16: “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame” (10:11). Some readers hear that promise already behind ‘I am not ashamed’.
passages.hard: What does ‘the righteousness of God’ mean, and how is a person ‘justified’? These two verses open the questions that divide churches most about Romans. Lutheran and Reformed churches stress God's verdict: the believer is declared righteous for Christ's sake. The Catholic Church teaches that God's verdict and a real inner renewal belong together. The Orthodox churches see salvation above all as union with God. Scholars also differ on whether ‘the righteousness of God’ is mainly a gift to us or God's own faithfulness. The book page sets out each view in its holders' own terms, and these notes do not choose. All agree that it is God's righteousness, revealed in the gospel, and received by faith.
passages.asks: Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel. Ask where you are: in what company, at work, at school, among clever friends, you would rather it did not come up. Then read Habakkuk's line again. It was given to a man waiting through a disaster for God to act. Ask what it would mean for you to live by trust while you wait.

passages.t: The truth pushed away, and glory exchanged
passages.happening:
Paul begins his long account of what is wrong with the world. It runs from here to 3:20.

“The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness” (verse 18). What may be known about God is plain to people, because God has made it plain (verse 19).

“For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse” (verse 20).

They knew God, Paul says, but they did not honour him as God or give him thanks. Their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened (verse 21). They claimed to be wise and became fools (verse 22). They “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Paul's hearers lived surrounded by statues of the gods. In Rome they stood in temples, in the forum, at street corners and in homes, mostly in human form. In Egypt gods were shown as birds, animals and serpents. Everyone in the room had seen what verse 23 describes.

Jewish believers would also recognise the argument. A Jewish book called the Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek, probably in the century before Paul, makes the same case in chapters 13 and 14: people should have known the Maker from his works, idolatry is folly, and it leads to moral ruin. That book is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, though not in Protestant ones. Jewish hearers would have been nodding along. In chapter 2 Paul will turn to them.

‘Wrath’ is the Greek orgē. It does not mean a burst of temper. It means God's settled, just opposition to evil. Paul says it ‘is being revealed’: it is already at work now, not only on a last day.

Notice where Paul puts the root of the trouble. Not first in what people did with their bodies, but in what they did with God: they would not honour him or thank him (verse 21). Ingratitude comes before idolatry, and idolatry before everything else in the chapter.

‘Exchanged’ is a key word. It comes three times in the chapter (verses 23, 25, 26). Each time people trade something true for something false.
passages.ot:
The Psalms say that creation speaks of its Maker: “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1).

Verse 23 echoes Israel's own worst moment. At Sinai the people made a golden calf (Exodus 32:4), and a psalm remembers it: “They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox” (Psalm 106:20). Jeremiah says the same of his day: “My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols” (Jeremiah 2:11). So Paul's description of Gentile idolatry already carries the memory of Israel's.

Paul's list, man and birds and animals and crawling things, follows the warning of Deuteronomy against making an idol “in the likeness of a male or female”, of any beast or bird, or “of any creature that crawls on the ground” (Deuteronomy 4:16-18). It also turns Genesis upside down. There God made humans in his image to rule over “the birds of the air” and “every creature that crawls upon it” (Genesis 1:26). Here humans bow down to images of the creatures they were made to care for.
passages.hard:
What does Paul mean by ‘the wrath of God’? He means God's just anger against evil, and he does not soften it. In this chapter he shows how it works now. Three times he says that God handed people over: “God gave them over” (verses 24 and 26) and “He gave them up” (verse 28). God lets people have what they have chosen, and what they chose turns on them. Paul also speaks of a coming “day of wrath” (2:5). He does not relish any of this. The same Greek verb, ‘hand over’, is used later of Jesus, who “was delivered over to death for our trespasses” (4:25). The answer to this chapter will be found there.

What can be known of God from creation? Paul says God's power and divine nature are ‘clearly seen’, so that people are ‘without excuse’. Christians draw different conclusions. The Catholic Church, at the First Vatican Council in 1870, taught that God can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason from the things he has made. Many Protestant confessions, such as the Belgic Confession, speak of a real knowledge of God from creation and providence, enough to leave people without excuse though not enough to save. Karl Barth, in 1934, answered his fellow theologian Emil Brunner with a sharp ‘No’, arguing that God is truly known only where he reveals himself in Christ. These notes do not choose. Paul's own point is not that people reason their way up to God. It is that they knew enough, and pushed it away.
passages.asks: Paul puts ingratitude at the root of the world's trouble. Ask when you last thanked God for something ordinary, and what you tend to give your thanks and trust to instead. An idol is not only a statue. It is anything you look to for what only God can give. Ask what yours might be.

passages.happening:
“Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity for the dishonoring of their bodies with one another” (verse 24). “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (verse 25).

For this reason, Paul says, God gave them over to dishonourable passions. Women “exchanged natural relations for unnatural ones” (verse 26). In the same way men gave up natural relations with women and “burned with lust for one another” (verse 27). Men committed indecent acts with other men and received in themselves the due penalty for their error (verse 27).

Since they did not think it worth acknowledging God, “He gave them up to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done” (verse 28).

Then comes a long list. People are filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed and depravity, full of envy, murder, strife, deceit and malice. They are gossips, slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant and boastful. They invent new forms of evil and disobey their parents. They are senseless, faithless, heartless and merciless (verses 29-31).

They know God's righteous decree that such things deserve death, yet they not only keep doing them, they approve of others who do (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The passage moves in three steps, each with the same pattern: people make an exchange, and God hands them over (verses 24, 26, 28). The judgment Paul describes is not lightning from the sky. It is God letting people go where they insist on going.

Lists of vices like the one in verses 29 to 31 were a common form in both Jewish and Greek moral teaching. Hearers knew the form. What they may not have expected is how wide this one is. It begins with greed and envy. It includes gossip, slander, arrogance, boasting and disobedience to parents. Murder sits beside gossip. No one in the room could hear it and stand outside it.

Jewish teaching of the time often linked idolatry and sexual sin as the twin marks of the Gentile world. The Wisdom of Solomon calls the worship of idols the beginning of every evil, and counts adultery and other sexual sins among its fruits (Wisdom 14). Paul's Jewish hearers would have recognised that link too, and agreed with every word so far.

‘The due penalty for their error’ (verse 27) is best read inside Paul's argument: the exchange carries its own ruin within it. It is not a statement that any illness or hardship is God's punishment on a person.

Verse 32 makes a last turn. Worse than doing wrong is cheering it on: approving of those who do it. That too is a sin of the crowd as much as of the person.
passages.ot:
The pattern ‘gave them over’ has an echo in the Psalms. God says of Israel, when they would not listen, “So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices” (Psalm 81:12).

Many readers hear creation behind Paul's words. ‘Creature’ and ‘Creator’ (verse 25) point back to Genesis 1, where “male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). On the historic reading, Paul's ‘natural’ and ‘unnatural’ point back to that order of creation.

Paul's Jewish hearers also knew the law of Moses: “You must not lie with a man as with a woman” (Leviticus 18:22). The same law calls many of the sins in Paul's list wrong too: lying, slander, hatred in the heart, and dishonouring father and mother (Leviticus 19:11-18; Exodus 20:12).
passages.hard:
What does Paul say in verses 26 and 27, and how do Christians read it?

Paul names same-sex sexual relations as one outworking of the exchange he has been describing. Of men he says it in so many words (verse 27). Of women he says they ‘exchanged natural relations for unnatural ones’ (verse 26), which most readers take in the same sense. People who exchanged the Creator for created things also made this exchange. He calls these ‘dishonorable passions’ and ‘indecent acts’. These notes state that plainly and do not soften it.

Christians read the passage in more than one way. The historic reading of the church, and still the reading of most churches today, is that Paul speaks of same-sex sexual acts as such. On this reading ‘natural’ points back to God's creation of humanity as male and female (Genesis 1:27), so his words apply to every such relationship. Some Christians read it differently. They hold that Paul was addressing the practices of his own world, which they see as marked by excess and exploitation, and an ancient idea of nature, so that he was not speaking of faithful, committed same-sex relationships. Those who hold the historic reading answer that Paul's language reaches back to creation, not to particular abuses. These notes set out both readings. Faithful Christians disagree here, and these notes take no side.

Three things are plain on any reading. First, Paul's very next sentence turns the charge on the reader: “You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another” (2:1). Second, the list in verses 29 to 31 includes envy, gossip and disobedience to parents, so that no reader stands outside it. Paul's point is that “all have sinned” (3:23). Third, nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.

If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Read the list in verses 29 to 31 slowly, and stop at the words that describe you: envy, gossip, arrogance, boasting, a heart that will not show mercy. Ask which of them you excuse in yourself while you notice them in others. Then ask what you approve of when others do it, and what that says about where your heart is turned.
